messages.subject: Question about `inla.spde2.matern` priors
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm trying to reproduce the analysis from a paper that used the `inla.spde2.matern` function. It looks like they haven't set the priors for the hyperparameters associated with the model since they run only:

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=meshfit, alpha=2)
res <- inla(formula, data=inla.stack.data(stk.full),
                 control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, A=inla.stack.A(stk.full)))

Therefore, I'm trying to figure out the default priors used with this latent model. (I'm aware that it is recommended to use `inla.spde2.pcmatern` instead, but I'm trying to reproduce some analysis from this paper I mentioned.)

When I look into `inla.docs("spde2", section = "latent")`, the documentation from the model is not available. In fact, when I go to the directory where INLA (I'm using version 23.08.18) is installed and ask for a list of files within "documentation/latent", none of the SPDE models is available (take a look below for reference)

> ls documentation/latent
ar.pdf              copy.pdf            intslope.pdf        rw2d-model.pdf
ar1.pdf             crw2.pdf            linear.pdf          rw2d.pdf
ar1c.pdf            dmatern.pdf         log1exp.pdf         rw2diid.pdf
besag.pdf           fgn.pdf             logdist.pdf         rw2dx3-model.pdf
besag2.pdf          generic0.pdf        matern2d.pdf        scopy.pdf
besagproper-OLD.pdf generic1.pdf        meb.pdf             seasonal.pdf
besagproper.pdf     generic2.pdf        mec-details.pdf     sigm.pdf
besagproper2.pdf    generic3.pdf        mec.pdf             slm.pdf
bym.pdf             iid.pdf             ou.pdf              wishard.pdf
bym2.pdf            iid123d.pdf         rgeneric.pdf        z.pdf
cgeneric.pdf        iidkd.pdf           rw1.pdf
clinear.pdf         indep.pdf           rw2.pdf

I noticed the default priors for the latent model "matern2d" (matern on a lattice) are
log(tau) \sim log-gamma(1, 5e-05), and
log(range) \sim log-gamma(1, 0.01).

My question is, do the same default priors hold for `inla.spde2.matern`?

Thanks,
Lucas.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about `inla.spde2.matern` priors
messages.body_plain:
The priors for the internal “theta” parameters can be found via inla.models()$latent$spde2, I think, but that won’t be very helpful for you, since the internal representation depends on some of the arguments to inla.spde2.matern() itself.
I think we did write about the default priors in the JSS paper on the spde2 interface, although we there promoted an alternative approach where one would explicitly parameterise the model in terms of log(range) and log(variance) instead of log(kappa) and log(tau).  Nowadays, the pcmatern implementation essentially uses the alternative approach (but with std.dev <http://std.dev>. instead of variance.  In hindsight, I wish I wouldn’t have allowed any default priors for inla.spde2.matern()…
It should however be more clear if you follow the code itself; I can take a look when I’m at my computer next.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about `inla.spde2.matern` priors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I took a look at the code, and the default parameter setup for inla.spde2.matern is in the param2.matern.orig() function. The default nominal variance is set to 1, meaning it tries to set the prior median for the marginal variance to 1. The default prior median range is constructed to be the approximate mesh diameter divided by 5 ( *0.2 in the code). The default prior precision on the log scale is 0.1.
If you want to replicate results where they’ve used the default settings, you’ll therefore need the same mesh, or at least know its approximate diameter. For details of the default prior construction, see the code, in rinla/R/spde2.R of the r-inla git repo.

Finn

> Hi,
> I took a look at the code, and the default parameter setup for inla.spde2.matern is in the param2.matern.orig() function. The default nominal variance is set to 1, meaning it tries to set the prior median for the marginal variance to 1. The default prior median range is constructed to be the approximate mesh diameter divided by 5 ( *0.2 in the code). The default prior precision on the log scale is 0.1.
> If you want to replicate results where they’ve used the default settings, you’ll therefore need the same mesh, or at least know its approximate diameter. For details of the default prior construction, see the code, in rinla/R/spde2.R of the r-inla git repo.

> > I think we did write about the default priors in the JSS paper on the spde2 interface, although we there promoted an alternative approach where one would explicitly parameterise the model in terms of log(range) and log(variance) instead of log(kappa) and log(tau). messages.subject: spatial covariates at integration points: INLA vs inlabru
messages.subject_clean: spatial covariates at integration points: INLA vs inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This is more of a question regarding model fitting rather than an issue I have with my code. I am trying to build a point process model that includes several of continuous covariates along with a spde component. At first I started creating these models using the R-INLA package but have recently transition to the inlabru package due to it ease with model development and prediction.

However, now I am confused how adding spatial covariates between the packages differ between the packages, particularly at the integration points? From Krainski et al. (2019), their example of adding spatial covariates to a LGCP model <https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-lcox.html#sec:lcoxcov> indicates that the "For model fitting, we must know the value of the covariate at the location points and integration points" for which they that explicitly in their example. The inlabru example of adding in continuous spatial covariates <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_covars.html#continuous-covariates> does not show how the covariates values are associated with the integration points. The inlabru example only shows extracting the continuous spatial covariates at the locations (through the function f.elev) but not at the integration points. This makes me curious what is inlabru doing differently? I am familiar with the Simpson et al. (2013) method and point process models (using a glm framework for example) where the quadratures are also given values of the spatial covariate. I saw from this thread <https://groups.google.com/u/1/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/0bBC9bVV-L4?pli=1> that inlabru does not apply the Simpson method but rather approximates the LGCP a bit differently (and more accurately!). Would it be possible to explain what inlabru is doing regarding spatial covariates at the integration points (I am an ecologist, so a more intuitive explanation may better help my understanding). Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Nima

messages.subject: implement non-stationarity
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I implemented a non-stationary spde model the following way:

spde.nonstat<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh, B.tau=cbind(0, 0, 0, 1, values_on_mesh),
                                B.kappa=cbind(0, 1, values_on_mesh, 0, 0),
                                theta.prior.mean=rep(0,4),
                                theta.prior.prec=rep(1,4))

and I wonder if this is correct, as the internal representation in INLA is theta_1=log(tau) and theta_2=log(kappa) and in my opinion this is not coherent with how I did it, which is
log(tau)=theta_3+ values_on_mesh*theta_4
log(kappa)=theta_1+values_on_mesh*theta_2.

Looking forward to your help. Thank you.

Corinna

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] implement non-stationarity
messages.body_plain:
The internal representation is only theta_1=log(tau) when B.tau =
cbind(0, 1, 0); the internal representation is _defined_ by the
user-supplied B.tau and B.kappa matrices.  Your representation is
precisely the intended way to extend this model to non-stationarity.
See the Details section of ?inla.spde2.matern, which defines the exact
construction.   The inla.spde.result() method uses the B-matrices to
compute the nominal range and variance (or the log() of them) also in
the non-stationary case.
However, the tau&kappa parameterisation isn't the ideal way to
represent nonstationarity since it's hard to control the variance
behaviour (it depends on both kappa and tau), and there are several
solutions to this.  One can be implemented using the existing
inla.spde2.matern function, but the best solution will require a new
internal model, that we're working on.

For the inla.spde2.matern() interface, there is a better way to
parameterise the existing implementation to get at least partial
separation between range and variance; using the approach from the
2015 JSS paper that uses "nominal range" and "nominal standard
deviation" as the basis for the parameterisation isn't perfect in the
non-stationary case, but it should be more well behaved than the pure
tau/kappa parameterisation. See pages 4-6 fo
https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19 that includes the
derivation of the needed B.tau and B.kappa parameters.

Of course, using a non-stationary extension of the PC-prior model for
the covariance parameters would be preferable, and that's part of what
one of my PhD students is currently working on.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial covariates at integration points: INLA vs inlabru
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] spatial covariates at integration points: INLA vs inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

in the continuous spatial covariates vignette, the initial version was
confusing on this point; the current version is a bit better, but
still not ideal; if you look at the "vegetation" covariate instead it
should be clearer; that that covariate takes discrete values is not
relevant to how it's accessed; the f.eval() could be used for either
discrete or continuous covariates; the "continuous" aspect is that
_space_ is treated as continuous.  Instead of
  elev(f.elev(coordinates(.data.)), model = "linear")
use
  elev(gcov$elevation, model = "linear")

This also preserves any crs information, so that you don't
accidentally end up evaluating the covariate in the wrong place.

The automated covariate elevation calls the eval_spatial() function,
which is essentially an encapsulation of the old "f.covar()" function
examples.  We still present the "f.covar()" approach in the vignette
to show how to do it if the eval_spatial() method for some reason
doesn't do what's needed in any particular special case.

When it comes to the Simpson et al (2013) paper, inlabry _does_ apply
that method, and it's rather several other examples that incorrectly
describe what that method is. The Simpson et al method uses the
lambda(s) values at each observed point for the \sum_i
log(lambda(y_i)) part of the likelihood, and the values of lambda(s)
at the integration points for the integral approximation part.
Methods that use aggregated counts at each vertex are different, and
_not_ what we developed in Simpson et al.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] implement non-stationarity
messages.body_plain:
The b_k(tau) = -b_k(kappa) part is needed if one wants to control the
range separately from the marginal variance.  Both approaches give
"valid" models, but the interpretation and properties are different.
This is because in the basic (kappa^2 - Delta)^{alpha/2} (tau x) = W
model, the marginal variance is proportional to 1/(kappa^{2\alpha - d}
* tau^2). So scaling tau by kappa^{\alpha-d/2} gives a parameter
that's proportional to 1/std.dev <http://std.dev> in the stationary case.
In the non-stationary case, the relationship is more complicated, but
similar. (there's a different model that has some more clear
theoretical underpinnings for decoupling variance and range, but it
doesn't fit in the spde2 implementation structure).

Finn

No, B.tau = (*, 0 0 a, b), B.kappa = (* ,c, d, 0 0) does _not_
separate range and variance at all. For that, you need the range
parameters to also influence the tau construction;
something like
B.tau = cbind(*, +1, +values, -1, -values)
B.kappa = cbind(*, -1, -values, 0, 0)
based on equations 11 and 9 in the JSS paper. That lets theta1 and
theta2 control the log(range), and theta3 and theta4 control the
log(marginal standard deviation).

Finn

messages.subject: Formulation of Knorr-Held (KH) models
messages.body_plain:
There seem to be two ways of using INLA to estimate
Knorr-Held spacetime models. One is with Elias Krainski's
inla.knmodels function. The other, as exemplified (eg) in
Blangiardo+Cameletti (B+C), is to use INLA's group feature.
In this connection, I have some questions: apologies in
advance if these are dumb, but on the other hand, they
should be easy to answer!

I. In the group (B+C) specification, does it matter which
(space or time) index is the first f-argument and which is
specified in the "group" option, as long as you get the
other settings to match up correctly? If it *does* matter,
which way is correct?  (I've seen both).

II. Everything I've read about KH models suggests that for
Types 2--4 there's an issue of rank deficiency that needs
to be addressed. Elias Krainski does this explicitly in
knmodels; B+C, as far as I can see, do not. Doesn't this mean
that there's a potential identification problem with B+C-type
specifications? If not, is there a simple explanation as to why not?

III. Does it make sense to estimate a KH Type-I spacetime
model when we have family="gaussian"? In that case wouldn't
we have 2 essentially identical iid effects so that only one
is identified? (Note that in the examples I've seen,
including B+C themselves, the family is Poisson, so this issue
doesn't arise for them).

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Formulation of Knorr-Held (KH) models
messages.body_plain:
1. In principle/theory, it doesn’t matter which of space and time is the main part and which is the group part of the specification, but in practice, space is almost always better to have as the main part (in particular for more general space-time models; K-H models are a somewhat odd special case)

2. Yes, the K-H models are meant to have constraints imposed on them to handle the rank deficiency; the theory is based on that, so implementation that don’t handle the rank deficiency actually don’t implement the K-H models, but rather the rank-deficient “proto-models” involved in the K-H model definitions. These models _can_ be ok as priors if the data itself is sufficiently informative, but it can easily lead to rank-deficient posterior distributions. Conclusion; Elias implementation should be preferred if one specifically wants the original K-H models.

Now, I don’t use those models myself, since the complex rank-deficiency makes the models extremely hard to I interpret (I prefer having proper priors, either separable with matern*ar1 or ar2, or nonseparable, like in INLAspacetime), but yes, if Type 1 models are simply completely independent iid variables, then combining that with additive Gaussian noise requires additional information to get an identifiable model.

Finn

messages.subject: compute quotient of two predictions/parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit a spatially-varying coefficient model to some spatiotemporal mortality data I have for counties. I'm specifically interested in fitting this model with race as a covariate and allowing the slope estimates for race to vary spatially and through time. I want to ultimately compute the ratio of deaths in one race category to my "baseline" race category in a given county in a given year and I'm interested in estimating the probability that this ratio is > or < 1.

It seemed like setting up this model in INLA might be the  best way to go about it, but I'm unsure of how to compute the ratios of mortality rates for each county at each time point.

Here's some example code using SIR for cancer in Ohio to set up this model. I'm hoping someone could help me determine the next steps for finding the estimates for mortality ratios. If I were doing this in Stan, I imagine I'd just compute the ratio in the generated quantities block but working with posteriors in INLA is a little more opaque to me right now.

library(INLA)
library(tidyr)
library(spdep)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(SpatialEpi)
library(SpatialEpiApp)

# Import and set up data
namecsv <- "SpatialEpiApp/data/Ohio/dataohiocomplete.csv"
dohio <- read.csv(system.file(namecsv, package = "SpatialEpiApp"))
head(dohio)
nameshp <- system.file(
  "SpatialEpiApp/data/Ohio/fe_2007_39_county/fe_2007_39_county.shp",
  package = "SpatialEpiApp")
map <- read_sf(nameshp)

d <- aggregate(
  x = dohio$y,
  by = list(county = dohio$NAME, year = dohio$year, gender = dohio$gender),
  FUN = sum
)
names(d) <- c("county", "year", 'gender', "Y")

dohio <- dohio[order(
  dohio$county,
  dohio$year,
  dohio$race,
  dohio$gender
), ]

E <- expected(
  population = dohio$n,
  cases = dohio$y,
  n.strata = 2
)
nyears <- length(unique(dohio$year))
countiesE <- rep(unique(dohio$NAME),
                 each = nyears * 2)

ncounties <- length(unique(dohio$NAME))
yearsE <- rep(unique(dohio$year),
              times = ncounties * 2)

dE <- data.frame(gender = c(1, 2), county = countiesE, year = yearsE, E = E)

d <- left_join(d, dE, by = c("county", "year", 'gender'))

d$SIR <- d$Y / d$E

nb <- poly2nb(map)
head(nb)
nb2INLA("map.adj", nb)
g <- inla.read.graph(filename = "map.adj")

d$idarea <- as.numeric(as.factor(d$county))
d$gender <- as.factor(d$gender)
d$idarea2 <- d$idarea1 <- d$idarea
d$idtime <- 1 + d$year - min(d$year)

# Want to model SIR by gender allowing the slopes for gender to vary spatially
# and for the time trend to vary spatially
formula <- Y ~ -1 +
  f(idarea, model = "bym", graph = g, scale.model = TRUE) +
  f(idarea1, gender, model = 'bym', graph = g, scale.model = TRUE) +
  f(idarea2, idtime, model = "bym", graph = g, scale.model = TRUE)

res <- inla(formula,
            family = "poisson", data = d, E = E,
            control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)
)
summary(res)

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I think you mean that you want the difference between two linear
predictors, since you're with poisson data and using a log-link, so that

risk = exp(lin.predictor)

hence ratios becomes differences.

I made some changes in your code, which you can check out.

since 'gender' (and later 'race') is a factor, it does not make sense to
use a varying regresssion, but its better to say that both genders has
similar response with some correlation (this is 'group=gender' argument;
see the book by Virgilio on www.r-inla.org <http://www.r-inla.org>)

also the bym model (or better the bym2) as buildt-in also an iid random
effect, its better not to use those in this setting.

I guess your example is more of a toy one, and you can follow the same
idea in your real example.

its benefitial to scale the covariates, like time, as you have set the
intercept to 0, otherwise, it does not make sense...

anyway, this is was I guess you want. otherwise let us know

H

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Apologies if this message comes through twice. I replied to the initial email, but I think I may have needed to reply in the discussion for it to properly show up. Thank you for your help - it's helped clarify my issue a bit. You are correct, the example I gave you is a toy example. It may not have been the best example to use I'm modeling something slightly different. Let me try and explain again with more mathematical notation to clarify my goals.

I have data on the counts of mortality events in group k in county j in year t, as well as the total population for group k in county j in year t. I have reason to believe that the mortality rates are different in each group k across both time t and space j, so I want to model these differences. The model I think I want is:

log(count_jkt / population_jkt) = alpha_jkt
log(count_jkt) = log(population_jkt) + alpha_jkt

Where log(population_jkt) is the offset and alpha_jkt is the group k intercept in county j at year t and could be decomposed into

log(count_jkt) = log(population_jkt) +  (b_k + u_kj + v_kj + gamma_kt + phi_kt + delta_kjt)

where b_k would be the group k intercept, u_kj is the spatially structured residual for group k in county j modeled with iCAR prior, v_kj would be the unstructured spatial residual for group k in county j, gamma_kt  would be the temporal effect for group k in year t and phi_kt would be a Guassian exchangeable prior for group k in year t. Delta_kjt would be a term to allow the spatial and temporal effects for group k to interact, specifically u_kj and gamma_kt (Type 4 interaction according to the Blangiardo and Cameletti 2015 book, which is what I'm using heavily as a reference, along with this article https://doi.org/10.1080/19475683.2020.1782469).

This model could be rewritten as:
count_jkt / population_jkt = exp(b_k + u_kj + v_kj + gamma_kt + phi_kt + delta_kjt)
If I have k = 3 groups, what I am interested in computing are the ratios of rates in group 2 to group 1 and rates in group 3 to group 1 in each county j and year t:
(count_2jt / population_2jt) / (count_1jt / population_1jt) and  (count_3jt / population_3jt) / (count_1jt / population_1jt)

Those ratios should be equivalent to:
exp(b_2 + u_2j + v_2j + gamma_2t + phi_2t + delta_2j) / exp(b_1  + u_1j + v_1j + gamma_1t + phi_1t + delta_1jt)

>From those ratios, I want to compute the probability that the ratios are >1 or <1 in each county j at time t.

If I have a variable race that represents my different groups then I think the model formula should look something like this, although I'm not confident it is correct:
formula <- counts ~ offset(log(population)) +
   f(areaID, model = 'bym', graph = g, group = race) +
   f(yearID, model = 'rw', group = race) +
   f(yearID2, model = 'iid', group = race) +
   f(areaID_interaction, model = 'besag', graph = g, group = yearID_interaction, control.group=list(model = 'rw'))

If you have feedback on correctly specifying this model (or thoughts on if a different modeling approach would be more appropriate) and also how to go about calculating the ratios I described, I would appreciate it.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] compute quotient of two predictions/parameters
messages.body_plain:
You can use linear combinations as I described earlier, but I would,
please the offsets in the argument E, so instead of

y ~ offset(log(pop)) + ...

I would use

y ~ ...

with inla(..., E=pop)

then 'pop' does not enter in the linear predictor.

note that in general

	Prob( exp(x)/exp(y) > 1) = Prob(exp(x-y) > 1)
		= Prob(x-y > 0)

so you do not need the distribution of the ratio, on the difference, to
compute this.

you can also sample fromt the fitted model, see the vignette about this

sample-eval             The inla.posterior.sample.eval-function
                        (source, pdf)

as then its just to return

	(Predictor[idx] - Predictor[jdx])

where idx and jdx is the vector of indices for linear predictors you
want to compare, and take the mean

this should really be straight forward.

Best
H

> Where log(population_jkt) is the offset and alpha_jkt is the group k

messages.subject: guidance for the generic model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to benchmark the speed of R-INLA to use it as a baseline for a method we are developing, but I'm having trouble implementing it.

I have observations in 2D, and I am trying to fit a GMRF with a Matern kernel.

My plan is:
Use the finite differences method to discretize the field into a regular grid, and compute the sparse prior precision matrix. This is implemented in Python, and will be shared between the various methods in the benchmark. It saves the sparse matrix to disk.
Load the sparse precision matrix in R
Use the "generic" model and specify the precision matrix using the Cmatrix parameter
I couldn't find any guidance for using the generic model, but I tried the following:
precision <- readMM("prior_precision.mtx")
data <- read.csv("data.csv")
log_precision <- log(precision)
formula <- y ~ f(x, model = "generic", Cmatrix = log_precision)
inla(formula, data = data)

data.csv contains a column x which gives the row/column of the precision matrix that the data point corresponds to, and a column y which gives the observation value.

The above code crashes:
inla.mkl: src/inla.c:37061: inla_INLA_preopt_experimental: Assertion `ABS(res[1] - res[3]) < DMAX(1, ABS(res[1])) * 1e-6' failed.

My questions are:
Is this a sensible way of including R-INLA in the benchmark? Would R-INLA be faster if I performed the finite difference approximation in R-INLA, rather than passing in the sparse prior matrix?
Do you have any pointers for how to write the R-INLA portion of the code? Is the generic model the correct thing to use, and are their any examples of using it?

Many thanks for you help!

Oscar
https://oscarkey.github.io/

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] guidance for the generic model
messages.body_plain:
Apart from the general difficulty of benchmarking, the code is
strangely written:

> log_precision <- log(precision)
> formula <- y ~ f(x, model = "generic", Cmatrix = log_precision)

Cmatrix should be the precision matrix, and presumably your
"precision" is that matrix, so it's not clear what you're trying to do
here.
I think you're looking for "generic0", documented in
INLA::inla.doc("generic0"), that by default has a scaling parameter
that's estimated. You can set that to a fixed value if you're not
estimating it, with f(..., hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1),
fixed=TRUE)))
but then if your model only has this component, there isn't anything
for inla to do except compute the kriging means and variances, and the
timings will mostly be overhead costs.

Finn

Hi,
your email had ended up in my spam folder so I didn't see it yesterday.

For normal distance sampling models, we use "distance" as an explicit
dimension, like in the examples at
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_distancesampling.html
where the "log_hn" and "log_hr" functions define how the detectability
depends on distance.

In your case, it seems you have some model in mind (I don't recall the
details of the specific Martino paper and you didn't provide a
link/reference) where you want "log_detect_sightings" to depend
directly on location instead of distance. You need to provide more
information about it for us to be able to help; it's impossible to
know how to write the code without knowing what mathematical model
needs to be implemented.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Issues with eval_spatial
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

with the recent inlabru devel versions, you can let the component handle the N(0,1)-->Exp(...) transformation, making the code a bit clearer.
Rewriting the code with that feature gives this:

log_detect = function(xy, scale, shift)
{
   dens <- eval_spatial(effort_final, where = xy)

  # print(dens)

  dens[is.na <http://is.na>(dens)] <- 0

  # bru_fill_missing should now be fixed, so you can use
  # dens <- bru_fill_missing(effort_final, xy, dens)

  pnorm(dens / scale - shift, log.p = TRUE)
}

bm_rexp <- bru_mapper_marginal(qexp, pexp, dexp, rate = 1)

cmp = ~ Intercept(1) +
  SPDE(main = geometry, model = matern) +
  bathy_s(bathy_rast$bathy_s) +

  effort_scale(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_rexp) +

  effort_shift(1, prec.linear = 1)

# Define the formula for the two observed processes
formula = geometry ~
  Intercept - 11 +
  bathy_s  +
  SPDE +
  log_detect(geometry,effort_scale,effort_shift)

The only logic difference in the above code compared with yours is that effort_scale will now behave as an exponentially distributed variable, so I would expect it to behave in the same way.
The model is only vaguely identifiable, as if one increases effort_shift (making the pnorm() smaller) and increases SPDE and/or Intercept and/or bathy_s, the predictor can remain the same.
That means that the prior distributions become _very_ important, so you'll want to carefully consider the effort_shift prec.linear value, the effort_scale rate value, the "Intercept - 11" shift construction, and potentially also the initial values since they control the linearisation point for the initial inlabru iteration.
bru_initial = list(effort_scale=0) corresponds to the prior median. You can convert from and to the internal scale with
ibm_eval(bm_rexp, NULL, state = internal_value)
ibm_eval(bm_rexp, NULL, state = effect_value, reverse = TRUE)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much for the advice.
However, with these changes, I still get the same error. I'm afraid the issue might be with the 'geometry' in 'log_detect'.
Shouldn't the function work row by row? This way, the result of 'dens' is always a matrix.

In the previous version, the code was defined as follows:

# Transformation function the the \xi paramters

qexppnorm <- function(x, rate){
  qexp(pnorm(x, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE),
       rate = rate,
       log.p = TRUE,
       lower.tail = FALSE)
}

f.fill = function(x,y, covar)
{
  spp <- SpatialPoints(data.frame(x=x,y=y),
                       proj4string = CRS(proj_utm_km))
  v <- over(spp, covar)
  v[is.na <http://is.na>(v)] <- 0 # NAs are a problem! Remove them
  return(v[,1])
}

cmp = ~ Intercept(1) +

  SPDE(main = coordinates, model = matern) +

  bathy_s(bathy_rast$bathy_s) +
  effort_scale(1, prec.linear = 1) +
  effort_shift(1, prec.linear = 1)

# Define the formula for the two observed processes

formula = coordinates ~

  Intercept - 11 +
  bathy_s  +
  SPDE +

  log_detect(x,y,effort_scale,effort_shift)

# Finally set things together and run the model
bru_options_set(bru_verbose = 1)

fit <- lgcp(components = cmp,
            sight_terra,
            samplers = poly,

            domain = list(coordinates = mesh),

            formula = formula,
            options = list(verbose = F))

With `sight_terra` as a `SpatialPixelDataFrame`

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Issues with eval_spatial
messages.body_plain:
eval_spatial() should return a vector, not a matrix.
“geometry” is just the sf variable that holds the points where it should be evaluated.
I’d rather not mix in sp objects in the discussion when troubleshooting sf code.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] whats the difference between inla.mode="classic" and ="experimental"?
messages.body_plain:
The "experimental" mode is the old name for the current default
"compact" mode (default since around Dec/Jan 2022/23 I believe).
It is based on a variational approximation in the final calculation
steps (the inner Laplace approximation is still there); see
  https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167947323000038
that refers to
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.12945
for further details.

Finn

I know river networks has been done using the barrier model, which is
now reimplemented in the add-on package

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] guidance for the generic model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

if that's all you're using it for, I suspect calling inla.qsolve() and
inla.qinv() might be preferable. It still involves writing the matrix
to disk (internally in the inla code), but it skips everything else.
You just need to construct the conditional precision matrix; Q_cond =
Q_x + A' Q_e A, where the observation model was y = A x + e, with e ~
N(0, Q_e^-1).
diag(inla.qinv(Q_cond)) will give you the conditional marginal
variances.  inla.qsolve(Q_cond,
the_RHS_of_the_precision_kriging_equations) gives you the kriging
mean.

Finn

messages.subject: qqplot for tweedie model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Could anybody give me a hand in creating a qqplot for a tweedie model? I have spent a terrible amount of time with something that I feel somebody could do in minutes if not seconds.

Example code:

library(inlabru)
library(tweedie)

n <-100
x <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.2)
eta <- 1 + .5*x #- 7.1*x^2
mu <- exp(eta)
plot(x,mu)
p <- 1.1
phi <- 1.75
y <- numeric(n)
for(i in 1:n) {
  y[i] <- rtweedie(1, xi = p, mu = mu[i], phi = phi)
  }

r <- bru(y ~ 1 + f(x,model="linear"), data = data.frame(y, x),
          family = "tweedie")

Cheers,
iosu

messages.subject: LGCP in INLA vs inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been fitting a LGCP model with a SPDE defining the spatial random effect and a mixture of linear and non-linear spatial covariates.

When I fit the model in inlabru, I use a SpatialPointsDF for the coordinates and a rasterization of my covariates in a SpatialPixelsDF format. The trouble is, the effect of the SPDE is null (the overall intensity plot looks reasonable as do the covariate effects) but it has an obvious pattern when included in the model on its own. I have tried different meshes and variations in the prior parameters with no luck. Is this because the spatial covariates are capturing all of the underlying pattern? (I struggle to believe this is the case as I have rasterized the covariates and lost some resolution in doing so).

When I fit the model in INLA, I keep my data in its original format (SpatialPolygonsDF) and model the count ~ covariates + SPDE (with the weights defined as the area of each polygon), getting a nice intensity value per polygon as a result. The outputs here (mean intensity, effect of spatial field, and covariate effects) all look good/reasonable.

I am wondering as to the difference - and why the effect of my spatial random field might be nullified when using inlabru.

And also if it would be possible to keep the SpatialPolygonsDF of covariates when fitting the LGCP in inlabru.

Finally - in terms of residual analysis; I followed the vignette Residual Analysis of spatial point process models using Bayesian methods • inlabru (inlabru-org.github.io) <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_residuals.html> for my inlabru LGCP. If I wanted to do this for my INLA LGCP (as this seems to produce the desired spatial random field pattern), are there methods/functions in place that translate this vignette for INLA models? Or would it be a manual job?

Apologies for the lengthy post, any help is greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Erin

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] LGCP in INLA vs inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Hi Erin,

from 2.9.0 (and 2.8.0, but with some automation issues) inlabru
handles polygon based covariates via the eval_spatial() methods; if
you supply a SPolygonsDF or an sf object with polygons, it will call
eval_spatial() to extract the covariates, so you don't need to
pre-rasterize them.

Have you tried running the count based model in inlabru as well, to
check if there's some inlabru specific issue also with that one?  For
example, the default intercept prior is different in plain inla and in
inlabru, as in inlabru it's treated the same as other covariates, and
this can change the estimates a bit.  However, I wouldn't expect it to
suppress the spde component, so that's probably not the issue.
What are the paraterm estimates? How close to zero is the estimated
spde standard deviation? (sigma in the pcmatern model). Also check
that your priors are sensible (in particular the range and sigma
parameters), taking note that sigma is the std.dev <http://std.dev>. for the Gaussian
field, and it's applied in an exponential link context, so large
values quickly become too large.

Finn

>
> Example code:
>
> library(inlabru)
> library(tweedie)
>
> n <-100
> x <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.2)
> eta <- 1 + .5*x #- 7.1*x^2
> mu <- exp(eta)
> plot(x,mu)
> p <- 1.1
> phi <- 1.75
> y <- numeric(n)
> for(i in 1:n) {
>   y[i] <- rtweedie(1, xi = p, mu = mu[i], phi = phi)
>   }
>
> r <- bru(y ~ 1 + f(x,model="linear"), data = data.frame(y, x),
>           family = "tweedie")
>
> Cheers,

For the residuals, we don't have any helper wrappers in the package
yet, just the code in the vignette and its .R helper file.
It's on the list of things to do...

To do it with a model run in plain inla you could in principle use the
same steps; the inlabru predict() calls simply call generate() +
summarisation code, and generate() is just a wrapper around
INLA::inla.posterior.sample().

Finn

these implementations are mainly to access the same internals as the
inla-program, hence there is quite some overhead as R write to file,
starts program as a separate process who read file, do comp, write to

1 x 1 sparse Matrix of class "dgTMatrix"

[1,] 1
Time difference of 0.327085495 secs

which is time taken for doing nothing.  so its reasonable to subtract
this constant from timings and similar with inla.qsolve().

well, it seems like you want to time sparse-factorisations, and not INLA
itself...  as Finn says, just be clear in your writing.

messages.subject: Prediction at validation stations
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would like to estimate a INLA model at 100 training stations and validate the model at 50 validation stations, which should be excluded from the training data set. Furthermore, for each station 20 observations are available in the training and validation data.
Unfortunately, I really struggle with it and I can not make it run. The code produces an error message including a hint, but somehow I can not make it work. I attached the code producing the error for replication. I am also not sure, if I specified the objects A_train/A_val and stack_train/stack_val correctly in the code.
I would really appreciate if you help me! Thank you so much!!!!!!

library(INLA)
###########################################
# ARTIFICAL EXAMPLE
###########################################
set.seed(123)

# number of observations (obs) for each location (loc)
t <- 20

# sample n = 100 locations to train
n <- 100
loc_train <- t(sapply(1:n, function(k) c(runif(1, 0, 5), runif(1, 0, 10))))
colnames(loc_train) <- c("x", "y")
# training data set including number of observation t, grid point (x, y),
# observation (obs) and covariate (cov)
df.loc_train <- data.frame(t = rep(1:t, each = nrow(loc_train)),
                           loc_train,
                           obs = rnorm(t*nrow(loc_train)),
                           cov = rnorm(t*nrow(loc_train)))

# sample n = 50 locations to validate
n <- 50
loc_val <- t(sapply(1:n, function(k) c(runif(1, 0, 5), runif(1, 0, 10))))
colnames(loc_val) <- c("x", "y")
# validation data set including number of observation t, grid point (x, y),
# observation (obs) and covariate (cov)
df.loc_val <- data.frame(t = rep(1:t, each = nrow(loc_val)),
                         loc_val,
                         obs = rnorm(t*nrow(loc_val)),
                         cov = rnorm(t*nrow(loc_val)))

# construct mesh for training locations
mesh <- inla.mesh.create(loc = loc_train,
                         cutoff = 0,
                         refine = list(max.edge = 10, min.angle = 0.01))
plot(mesh)
points(x = loc_train[, 1], y = loc_train[, 2], col = "red")
points(x = loc_val[, 1], y = loc_val[, 2], col = "blue")

# create spde
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh,
                          alpha = 2)

field.indices <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "field",
                                      n.spde = mesh$n,
                                      n.repl = t)

# observation matrix A for the training locations
A_train <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh,
                            loc = loc_train,
                            index = rep(1:nrow(loc_train), times = t),
                            repl = rep(1:t, each = nrow(loc_train)))

# observation matrix A for the validation locations
A_val <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh,
                          loc = loc_val,
                          index = rep(1:nrow(loc_val), times = t),
                          repl = rep(1:t, each = nrow(loc_val)))

stack_train <- inla.stack(data = list(Y = df.loc_train$obs),
                          A = list(A_train, 1),
                          effects = list(field.indices,
                                         list(cov = df.loc_train$cov)),
                          tag = "train")

stack_val <- inla.stack(data = list(Y = NA),
                        A = list(A_val, 1),
                        effects = list(field.indices,
                                       list(cov = df.loc_val$cov)),
                        tag = "val")

stack <- inla.stack(stack_train, stack_val)

fit <- inla(formula = Y ~ f(field, model = spde) + f(field, cov, model = spde),
            family = "gaussian",
            data = inla.stack.data(stack, spde=spde),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE),
            control.inla = control.inla(strategy = "auto"),
            control.compute = list(config = TRUE))

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prediction at validation stations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter,

your model formula has two conflicting latent component definitions.
If you wanted a model like
\eta(s) = u(s) + v(s) * cov(s)
for two independent spatial fields u and v, then you have to give the
component different names. In the plain INLA interface you need to do
that by having two differently named "field" index variables.
Also, you're constructing index variables for a temporally replicated
field, but you're not using that in the model definition, so it's not
entirely clear what model it is you're trying to implement.
If you were intending both u and v to be temporally replicated
(independent for each time point, but with time-constant covariance
parameters):

field.indices <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "field",
                                      n.spde = mesh$n,
                                      n.repl = t)

field_cov.indices <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "field_cov",

                                      n.spde = mesh$n,
                                      n.repl = t)

stack_train <- inla.stack(data = list(Y = df.loc_train$obs),
                          A = list(A_train,

Diagonal(nrow(df.loc_train), df.loc_train$cov) %*% A_train,
                          effects = list(field.indices, field_cov.indices),
                          tag = "train")

stack_val <- ...

stack <- inla.stack(stack_train, stack_val)

fit <- inla(formula = Y ~ f(field, model = spde, replicate =
field.repl) + f(field_cov, model = spde, replicate = field_cov.repl),

            family = "gaussian",
            data = inla.stack.data(stack, spde=spde),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE),
            control.inla = control.inla(strategy = "auto"),
            control.compute = list(config = TRUE))

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] bgev prediction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Corinna,

the observed value will usually have more variability than the posterior mean of the location parameter for the observation model.

For example:
Take a simpler case, with a predictor \eta_i observed with additive Gaussian noise, to get y_i = \eta_i + \epsilon_i, where \epsilon_i ~ N(0, \sigma^2)
Then even if we could perfectly estimate \eta_i, then the spread of values would be smaller than for y_i, because of the contribution from the \epsilon_i.

This is also the case for the bgev distribution model, and virtually _every_ observation model; furthermore, generally in spatial statistics when there's a Gaussian field involved in the model for \eta, the posterior mean for \eta will be fundamentally smoother across space than the observations, and have smaller variability.

The quetion I think you need to consider is instead whether the posterior predictive distribution for y_i resembles the observed values.
In the Gaussian case, one can simply add&subtract a quantile of the \epsilon-distribution, but for bgev I assume it would involve either posterior sampling on the data level, or some quantile calculations.  Posterior predictive sampling is the most general approach, as it allows any type of model.

Finn

in bym2

you asked for (which is a sign a to vague model...)

messages.subject: Joint models in INLA using "current value" parameterisation
messages.subject_clean: Joint models in INLA using "current value" parameterisation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am very new to INLA but interested to use it for joint modelling of longitudinal and survival outcomes. In particular I'm interesting in fitting joint models where the current value of the longitudinal outcome is included directly as a covariate in the survival model (as opposed to a shared random effect set-up).

After following some examples found in this paper: https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v100.i02 and elsewhere, I have tried to fit the same fairly simple joint model using both the JM package and via INLA (R code is attached), using the pbc.id <http://pbc.id> and pbc2 datasets from the JM package. Looking at the output, it seems like some of the parameter estimates are quite different between my two fitted models, so I think I am still going wrong when trying to translate the model to specify it in INLA.

Could anyone give me pointers on where I am going wrong here?

On a related note - could anyone give some intuition as to why the appropriate value for the "w" variable used to copy the linear predictor from the longitudinal model to the survival model is -1?

Any help or comments would be appreciated!

Kind regards,
Annabel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Erin,

I recall running into this error message before, or hearing from
someone else, and it was solved somehow.
Please provide at least the traceback() output and sessionInfo() as
that may help pin down the source.

loading Matrix with library(Matrix) solves the problem. If it does,
there's some code somewhere that is sensitive to S4 method issues...

session), since if it does it might be easier to debug your problem by
checking what's different in your code.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Apologies, I get an error when trying to add attachments for some reason. Would you mind if I sent them to you via email?
In terms of model definition;
bnd        <- spoly(data.frame(x = c(-1351.2, 1824.997, 1824.997, -1351.2), y = c(2679.225, 2679.225, 5074.243, 5074.243)))
^ I have defined my boundary from the extent of the boundary SPolygonsDF I have for my data, as I wanted to keep as close to the example as possible.
mesh     <- fm_mesh_2d_inla(boundary = bnd, max.edge = 100)
matern  <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh_fine, prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01), prior.range = c(1, 0.01))
^ I have found varying these parameters does not change anything in terms of the error

Jdf <- sf::st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = locations$x, y = locations$y),
  coords = c("x", "y")
)
Jdf$count <- as.numeric(Japan$LandslideC)
^ dataframe holding geometry and response variable

cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, matern)

fit <- bru(cmp, Jdf, family = "gaussian")
^I used "gaussian" for simplicity as I was just trying to run the model fit without getting the error

Thanks,
Erin

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I found the reason:

cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, matern)

should be

cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, model = matern)

You can see in the help text for the component constructor,
?component, that the model parameter "model" comes after "...". This
in R means that you have to name it explicitly.
Also, if it _had_ come before "...", it still wouldn't have been the
second argument (which is "weights", just like in ordinary INLA::f()
calls).

The cryptic error message came from inlabru attempting to compute the
derivative of the "product between the weights object and the latent
state", which is clearly undefined when "weights" has accidentally
become a "matern" model object.  I'm actually amazed that it got that
far in the code before trying to do something invalid with that object
without noticing.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I've now added some extra checks to the inlabru code to detect invalid
mapper inputs sooner and give more informative messages when it does;
the logic that lead to your specific error message is still a bit
non-intuitive, as it's not the inadvertent invalid "weights" input
that's detected, but rather that the lack of a model specification
lead to it defaulting to model="linear", which in turn makes the
main=geometry input invalid for the bru_mapper_linear() mapping!
The extra checks&messages are in inlabru from 2.9.0.9013, see
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/news/index.html

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] LGCP in INLA vs inlabru
messages.body_plain:
Ah my goodness! I can't believe I missed that. Thank you very much.
On that note.. the count-based model in inlabru now works as wonderfully as the count-based model in INLA, and it is just when using lgcp() that the spde component is suppressed.
Erin

On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 4:58:43 PM UTC+1 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I found the reason:
>
> cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, matern)
>
> should be
>
> cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, model = matern)
>
> You can see in the help text for the component constructor,
> ?component, that the model parameter "model" comes after "...". This
> in R means that you have to name it explicitly.
> Also, if it _had_ come before "...", it still wouldn't have been the
> second argument (which is "weights", just like in ordinary INLA::f()
> calls).
>
> The cryptic error message came from inlabru attempting to compute the
> derivative of the "product between the weights object and the latent
> state", which is clearly undefined when "weights" has accidentally
> become a "matern" model object. I'm actually amazed that it got that
> far in the code before trying to do something invalid with that object
> without noticing.
>
> Finn

messages.body_plain:
Progress!

Check all your crs info's; fm_crs(mesh), fm_crs(Jdf), etc, etc. and
make sure that your pcmatern range prior is in the same units as the
mesh.
Also check your pcmatern sigma prior is sensible (c(1, 0.01) should be
ok, but c(1, 0.01) would allow it to accept more variability into the
field).

Finn

>>
>> Hi,
>>
>> I found the reason:
>>
>> cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, matern)
>>
>> should be
>>
>> cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, model = matern)
>>
>> You can see in the help text for the component constructor,
>> ?component, that the model parameter "model" comes after "...". This
>> in R means that you have to name it explicitly.
>> Also, if it _had_ come before "...", it still wouldn't have been the
>> second argument (which is "weights", just like in ordinary INLA::f()
>> calls).
>>
>> The cryptic error message came from inlabru attempting to compute the
>> derivative of the "product between the weights object and the latent
>> state", which is clearly undefined when "weights" has accidentally
>> become a "matern" model object. I'm actually amazed that it got that
>> far in the code before trying to do something invalid with that object
>> without noticing.
>>
>> Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatotemporal dataset creation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fabio,

I am not sure if you want to sample from spatio-temporal models in the
discrete or in the continuous domain, even though the RandomFields
package is for the continuous domain case.

In the discrete domain case, the inla.knmodels.sample() can be used to
sample from the (scaled) separable (covariance/precision)
spatio-temporal models introduced in
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10960871/
and you can also easily build a variety of separable spatio temporal
models considering other spatial and temporal models in a similar
fashion building the precision matrix and then using the
inla.qsample() function.

In the continuous domain case, the new INLAspacetime package could be
considered for some of the separable and nonseparable spatio-temporal
models presented in https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04917

best regards,
Elias

messages.subject: INLA survival model formulation using inla.stack and multiple likelihoods
messages.subject_clean: INLA survival model formulation using inla.stack and multiple likelihoods
messages.body_plain:
Hi! I'm attempting to formulate a survival model jointly with a measurement error + exposure model (as in Muff et. al (2015) (https://www.jstor.org/stable/24771892) and more specifically Skarstein et. al (2023), example 4.3 (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/bimj.202300078)), but I would like to do this using inla.stacks. So it is a Weibull survival model with a measurement error model for one covariate, and that introduces two additional levels to the model. I have formulated the model successfully by specifying the matrices manually (this can be found here: https://emmaskarstein.github.io/Missing-data-and-measurement-error/missing_and_mismeasured_covariate.html#me-model-ignoring-missing-observations) So I feel like it should not be a problem using inla.stacks to structure the data instead, but I'm struggling with the structure of the survival response.

One option, following this example: https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-risk.html, would be to specify the time and event for inla.surv as separate vectors to the stack, and then call inla.surv directly in the formula. However, since I also need to include the responses for the measurement error model and exposure model in the formula, that won't work.

The other approach, more closely following my previous implementation using the matrices directly, would involve passing the inla.surv object as one list element to the stack data, together with two columns of NAs, and naming the list of all three of these Y. Then the formula could just have Y on the left hand side. However, when passing the inla.surv-object as one of the elements in a list as the data input in inla.stack, I get the error "Error in as.data.frame.default(x[[i]], optional = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = stringsAsFactors) : cannot coerce class ‘"inla.surv"’ to a data.frame".

I noticed the documentation for inla.stack says that the data argument should be a dataframe or a list of vectors, so I'm wondering if it is at all possible to structure the data for a survival model like this using stacks?

Here is some code to illustrate the issue (I've attached the whole code that continues this example in an R-file for further context):

# Exploring survival stacks

library(INLA)

n <- 100

t <- runif(n, 0, 10) # Survival time
d <- sample(c(0,1), n, replace = TRUE) # Survival event

x <- rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Covariate with measurement error
z <- rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Covariate without measurement error

data <- data.frame(t, d, x, z)

# Regression model of interest
# eta = beta.0 + beta.x*x + beta.z*z
Y.surv <- inla.surv(data$t, data$d)

stk_moi <- inla.stack(
    data = list(Y = list(Y.surv, rep(NA, n), rep(NA, n))), # THIS FAILS
    A = list(1),
    effects = list(
      list(beta.0 = rep(1, n),
           beta.x = 1:n,
           beta.z = data$z)),
    tag = "moi")

messages.body_plain:
Hi Emma,

currently, you will have to use inla.stack() to construct the data
that will be used as the _input_ to inla.surv(), i.e. first call
inla.stack() to setup all the input data, and then call any special
observation object constructors afterwards (e.g. directly in the
formula) using inla.stack.data(...), collecting them into a list in
the case of multiple observation families.,  like
list(data.frame(y=y), inla.surv(...)) ~ ...

We have started working on the needed internal code restructuring for
allowing each observation model to be built separately and only _then_
combined into a joint model; once this is done that will also allow
inla.surv() to be used in the inlabru interface (that _always_
constructs each observation model separately and combines them
afterwards), meaning that there would be no more need for the user to
call inla.stack() themselves (models with special observation
objects/functions is the only remaining use case for user-code
inla.stack() calls); if that step will be needed at all, it will be
done internally by inlabru, like it currently does with all other
models.

Finn

messages.subject: inla.stack Error: Mismatching row sizes
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I just can't find my error. I would be very grateful if you can help me

I am using:
R version 4.3.1 (RStudio 2023.06.2+561)
INLA version 23.09.09
on Mac 13.5.2

When running:

StackNB.mesh1 <- inla.stack(
  tag  = "FitNB",
  data = list(AllY = cbind(WISA_df_nNA$PosAnz_RBU_B0, NA)),
  A    = list(1, A1),
  effects = list(
    XNB = as.data.frame(X),
    wNB = w1.NB.index))

I get the error:

Error in parse.input.list(effects[[k]], input.ncol(A[[k]]), paste("Effect block ",  :
  Effect block 2:
Mismatching row sizes: 1578, n.A=1641

I think that I did not change anything relevant in the code and that this error does not occurred with NLA version 23.05.30-1.

Here the code to get to the stack:

Loc <- cbind(WISA_df_nNA$Xkm,WISA_df_nNA$Ykm)
lps <- coordinates(Polygone)
ID <- cut(lps[,1], quantile(lps[,1]), include.lowest=TRUE)
reg4 <- unionSpatialPolygons(Polygone, ID)
row.names(reg4)
reg4$ID <- levels(as.factor(ID))
bdry <- inla.sp2segment(reg4, crs = "+proj=utm +zone=33 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs")
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = Loc,boundary=bdry, cutoff=400 ,max.edge=750, crs = inla.CRS("+proj=utm +zone=33 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs"))

A1 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = Loc)
A2 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = Loc)

spde1   <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 2, crs = inla.CRS("+proj=utm +zone=33 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs"))
spde2   <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh, alpha = 2, crs = inla.CRS("+proj=utm +zone=33 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs"))

w1.NB.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 'wNB', n.spde  = spde1$n.spde)
w2.NB.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 'wNB', n.spde  = spde2$n.spde)

Hi Louis,

I'd recommend checking that your Loc variable really contains
coordinates in metres, as assumed by the crs specifications you use,
and not kilometres as indicated by the variable names Xkm, Ykm.

Also remove the crs argument in inla.spde2.matern() as it does nothing.

Note that the new inla version uses the fmesher package for mesh
handling, which in most cases does exactly the same as old code, but
also handles sf objects etc more transparently, making coordinate
system handling a bit safer/correct.

For your specific error message, check the size of Loc, mesh$n,
spde1$n.spde, str(A1), as well as str(w1.NB.index), and
nrow(WISA_df_nNA), as the size discrepancy likely comes from one of
those being incorrect.

Finn

messages.subject: fm_rcdt_2d_inla vs. inla.mesh.create differences
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for all the work extracting mesh construction to the fmesher package on CRAN.

I have noticed a difference in the meshes produced by fmesher::fm_rcdt_2d_inla() compared to INLA::inla.mesh.create() and INLA <= 23.06.29. See a minimal example below using fmesher.evolution to use the old code. The difference seems to be with the outer boundary and triangles between that boundary and the data. Is there an obvious set of arguments I can use to make these fmesher package meshes match the older INLA ones?

set.seed(1)
dat <- matrix(runif(200), ncol = 2L)
INLA::inla.setOption(fmesher.evolution = 1L)

packageVersion("INLA")
#> [1] '23.9.9'
packageVersion("fmesher")
#> [1] ‘0.1.2’

inla_mesh <- INLA::inla.mesh.create(
  dat,
  cutoff = 0.1
)
fmesher_mesh <- fmesher::fm_rcdt_2d_inla(
  dat,
  cutoff = 0.1
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(inla_mesh, asp = 1, main = NA);points(dat)
mtext("INLA::inla.mesh.create() & \nINLA <= INLA_23.06.29 \n fmesher.evolution = 1")
plot(fmesher_mesh);points(dat)
mtext("fmesher::fm_rcdt_2d_inla() | \nINLA >= INLA_23.08.18 \n fmesher.evolution = 2")

Resulting meshes:
https://i.imgur.com/ksc18LC.png

Separately, are there any plans to pull INLA::inla.spde2.matern() into fmesher or some other package hosted on CRAN?

Thanks,
Sean

Inla.spde2.matern itself doesn’t really make sense without inla, but the underlying code is already in fmesher; search for matern and/or precision in the fmesher documentation on github.io <http://github.io>.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] fm_rcdt_2d_inla vs. inla.mesh.create differences
messages.body_plain:
I've taken a quick look at the code&documentation, and the argument
would be extend=list(n=16) to get 16 outer points,

What you're experiencing is a difference in the handling of the case
extend=TRUE, where the fmesher version doesn't set any extension
defaults, causing the defaults to be set by the internal C++ code.
You can use extend = list() to regain the old behaviour until the next
fmesher version (I'll update fmesher on github today).

Interestingly though, both the old and new code have a
documentation/code mismatch in the defaults; the R documentation says
8 but the R code uses 16.
The discrepancy above is because the C++ code default follows the documentation!

Another thing to be aware of is that due to different floating point
behaviour on M1 processors, M1 systems can get different meshes than
on intel and amd. (This is not new behaviour for fmesher, but has
always been true for M1; it was just discovered when testing the
fmesher package for CRAN submission).
So make sure to write code that either doesn't rely on the specific
mesh, and store a specific mesh to disk if/when you need to make sure
it never changes.

Finn

Why don't you observe zero's? Because you can't observe them? Or because they are not possible? In the latter case a zero-truncated Poisson seems more relevant to me.

inla(
  f,
  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
  control.family = list(
    list(hyper = list(theta = list(initial = -11, fixed = TRUE)))
   )
)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: cenpoisson requirements
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

from reading inla.doc("cenpoisson"), I think there's an error in the
documentation, as it says that it deals with values being censored
inside the interval [L, H], but the cenpoisson2 documentation that is
the same except that it allows individual [L, H] values for each
observation seems to make it clear that it is values _outside_ the
interval that is censored.
However, both example codes actually do censor values inside the
intervals (replacing them with L), so there's a clear confusion there;
I'll check with Haavard.

However, what model you need depends on if you have censored
observations (values _outside_ [1,Inf] being censored, setting zeros
to 1), or rather _truncated_ observations, where you've observed Y
from a truncated Poisson distribution, Pr(Y=y | y>0)?  In that case
you can use zeroinflatedpoisson1 with a fixed small probability for
zero.

In either case, E is a known scaling constant, so that the Poisson
expectation is defined as E * exp(eta), where eta is the linear
predictor.
E is usually read as "exposure", and used to scale the model with
respect to some known quantity (e.g. population in many cases).

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] cenpoisson requirements
messages.body_plain:
In this case I think a truncated Poisson is more appropriate (with zeroinflatedpoisson0, like Thierry showed) than an LGCP, unless you do a joint "marked point process model" approach.

Adding zeros on a grid probabilty wouldn't be very helpful, as it would just give you a more expensive way to approximate a marked point process model, and might conflate "did not go there to look for things" with "did not find anything where I looked".

Finn

Hi Finn, thank you for the reply!

On Tuesday, 19 September 2023 at 15:39:29 UTC+2 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi Corinna,
>
> the observed value will usually have more variability than the posterior mean of the location parameter for the observation model.
>
> For example:
> Take a simpler case, with a predictor \eta_i observed with additive Gaussian noise, to get y_i = \eta_i + \epsilon_i, where \epsilon_i ~ N(0, \sigma^2)
> Then even if we could perfectly estimate \eta_i, then the spread of values would be smaller than for y_i, because of the contribution from the \epsilon_i.
>
> This is also the case for the bgev distribution model, and virtually _every_ observation model; furthermore, generally in spatial statistics when there's a Gaussian field involved in the model for \eta, the posterior mean for \eta will be fundamentally smoother across space than the observations, and have smaller variability.
>
> The quetion I think you need to consider is instead whether the posterior predictive distribution for y_i resembles the observed values.
> In the Gaussian case, one can simply add&subtract a quantile of the \epsilon-distribution, but for bgev I assume it would involve either posterior sampling on the data level, or some quantile calculations.  Posterior predictive sampling is the most general approach, as it allows any type of model.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] bgev prediction
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm not entirely sure what the question is, as the "predictive
posterior estimates" on the data level _is_ what you get by using
inla.posterior.sample to sample the latent variables and then from
that sample the data level.

But if you mean how to compare the posterior predictive samples to the
observed sample distribution, then there are several ways, depending
on the specific aspect being investigated (e.g. spatial prediction
would be treated differently to the "overall marginal distribution",
etc).
Might help if you have a more specific question in mind regarding what
aspect of the predictions you want to investigate; leave-site-out
prediction being one possible choice.

I believe there's one or more papers by Aki Vehtari and colleagues
about how to assess posterior predictive samples. (e.g. with
probability integral transform histograms and/or
Kolmogorov-Smirnov-type CDF difference comparisons, etc)

Finn

Dear all,

Thank you so much for your answers and clarifications. I understand what I have been struggling with now! I think indeed a zero-truncated model is most appropriate, as it runs very fast in INLA and gives good (spatial) fitting.

For reference:
inla_sp = inla(f,

                  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
                  control.family = list(

                    list(hyper = list(theta = list(initial = -11, fixed = TRUE)))),

                  data = inla.stack.data(StackFit),
                  control.compute = list(waic=T),

                  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(StackFit)))

kind regards,
Charlotte Taelman

> On 25 Sep 2023 at 15:27 +0200, Emma Skarstein <emmaskar...@gmail.com>, wrote:
> > Hi! I'm attempting to formulate a survival model jointly with a measurement error + exposure model (as in Muff et. al (2015) (https://www.jstor.org/stable/24771892) and more specifically Skarstein et. al (2023), example 4.3 (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/bimj.202300078)), but I would like to do this using inla.stacks. So it is a Weibull survival model with a measurement error model for one covariate, and that introduces two additional levels to the model. I have formulated the model successfully by specifying the matrices manually (this can be found here: https://emmaskarstein.github.io/Missing-data-and-measurement-error/missing_and_mismeasured_covariate.html#me-model-ignoring-missing-observations) So I feel like it should not be a problem using inla.stacks to structure the data instead, but I'm struggling with the structure of the survival response.
> >
> > One option, following this example: https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-risk.html, would be to specify the time and event for inla.surv as separate vectors to the stack, and then call inla.surv directly in the formula. However, since I also need to include the responses for the measurement error model and exposure model in the formula, that won't work.
> >
> > The other approach, more closely following my previous implementation using the matrices directly, would involve passing the inla.surv object as one list element to the stack data, together with two columns of NAs, and naming the list of all three of these Y. Then the formula could just have Y on the left hand side. However, when passing the inla.surv-object as one of the elements in a list as the data input in inla.stack, I get the error "Error in as.data.frame.default(x[[i]], optional = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = stringsAsFactors) : cannot coerce class ‘"inla.surv"’ to a data.frame".
> >
> > I noticed the documentation for inla.stack says that the data argument should be a dataframe or a list of vectors, so I'm wondering if it is at all possible to structure the data for a survival model like this using stacks?
> >
> > Here is some code to illustrate the issue (I've attached the whole code that continues this example in an R-file for further context):
> >
> > # Exploring survival stacks
> >
> > library(INLA)
> >
> > n <- 100
> >
> > t <- runif(n, 0, 10) # Survival time
> > d <- sample(c(0,1), n, replace = TRUE) # Survival event
> >
> > x <- rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Covariate with measurement error
> > z <- rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Covariate without measurement error
> >
> > data <- data.frame(t, d, x, z)
> >
> > # Regression model of interest
> > # eta = beta.0 + beta.x*x + beta.z*z
> > Y.surv <- inla.surv(data$t, data$d)
> >
> > stk_moi <- inla.stack(
> >     data = list(Y = list(Y.surv, rep(NA, n), rep(NA, n))), # THIS FAILS
> >     A = list(1),
> >     effects = list(
> >       list(beta.0 = rep(1, n),
> >            beta.x = 1:n,
> >            beta.z = data$z)),
> >     tag = "moi")
> >

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] cenpoisson requirements
messages.body_plain:
oops, the 'cenpoisson' is cencored in the way that observations in the
interval [L,H] is reported as L, say. this sometimes is done for privacy
reasons, where L=0 and H=5, say.

this is very very different from a case where 0's are not observed. so
there is no 'choice' here, the data collection process dictates what to
use.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you all for these comments! I'm looking forward to seeing the future INLA interface. I did also look a bit at INLAjoint when trying to figure this out, but since I want this code (in my package) to generalize to other families than just survival models, I think it may be just as well to specify them myself for now (at least for the simple survival models I have had to deal with so far). By just specifying the response in the formula as a list now it is working very nicely! I also realized that I could simplify the response in the stacks a bit: by naming each response vector I don't actually need to set the NA's, which makes the code a lot tidyer.

Best,
Emma

> > On 25 Sep 2023 at 15:27 +0200, Emma Skarstein <emmaskar...@gmail.com>, wrote:
> > > Hi! I'm attempting to formulate a survival model jointly with a measurement error + exposure model (as in Muff et. al (2015) (https://www.jstor.org/stable/24771892) and more specifically Skarstein et. al (2023), example 4.3 (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/bimj.202300078)), but I would like to do this using inla.stacks. So it is a Weibull survival model with a measurement error model for one covariate, and that introduces two additional levels to the model. I have formulated the model successfully by specifying the matrices manually (this can be found here: https://emmaskarstein.github.io/Missing-data-and-measurement-error/missing_and_mismeasured_covariate.html#me-model-ignoring-missing-observations) So I feel like it should not be a problem using inla.stacks to structure the data instead, but I'm struggling with the structure of the survival response.
> > >
> > > One option, following this example: https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/spde-gitbook/ch-risk.html, would be to specify the time and event for inla.surv as separate vectors to the stack, and then call inla.surv directly in the formula. However, since I also need to include the responses for the measurement error model and exposure model in the formula, that won't work.
> > >
> > > The other approach, more closely following my previous implementation using the matrices directly, would involve passing the inla.surv object as one list element to the stack data, together with two columns of NAs, and naming the list of all three of these Y. Then the formula could just have Y on the left hand side. However, when passing the inla.surv-object as one of the elements in a list as the data input in inla.stack, I get the error "Error in as.data.frame.default(x[[i]], optional = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = stringsAsFactors) : cannot coerce class ‘"inla.surv"’ to a data.frame".
> > >
> > > I noticed the documentation for inla.stack says that the data argument should be a dataframe or a list of vectors, so I'm wondering if it is at all possible to structure the data for a survival model like this using stacks?
> > >
> > > Here is some code to illustrate the issue (I've attached the whole code that continues this example in an R-file for further context):
> > >
> > > # Exploring survival stacks
> > >
> > > library(INLA)
> > >
> > > n <- 100
> > >
> > > t <- runif(n, 0, 10) # Survival time
> > > d <- sample(c(0,1), n, replace = TRUE) # Survival event
> > >
> > > x <- rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Covariate with measurement error
> > > z <- rnorm(n, 0, 1) # Covariate without measurement error
> > >
> > > data <- data.frame(t, d, x, z)
> > >
> > > # Regression model of interest
> > > # eta = beta.0 + beta.x*x + beta.z*z
> > > Y.surv <- inla.surv(data$t, data$d)
> > >
> > > stk_moi <- inla.stack(
> > >     data = list(Y = list(Y.surv, rep(NA, n), rep(NA, n))), # THIS FAILS
> > >     A = list(1),
> > >     effects = list(
> > >       list(beta.0 = rep(1, n),
> > >            beta.x = 1:n,
> > >            beta.z = data$z)),
> > >     tag = "moi")
> > >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Louis,
that size information is very useful;

I think you used something like length(Loc) instead of the intended
nrow(Loc), since the A1 matrix height is exactly half; 98244 vs 49122?
More importantly, the mesh size 14898 doesn't match the spde1 size,
14083, as you noted, and this should be impossible for the current and
past 2D mesh code (for 1D "meshes" they can be different, but in a
well-defined way).
This means that we can ignore all follow-up errors; the inla.stack
error message simply detected this problem.
Are you absolutely sure you generated the spde1 object from this mesh,
and that there was no warning message or other thing?

If you just type

  mesh

in the R console, what's the output?

Also,

  str(fm_basis(mesh, loc = Loc))

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Thanks,
I now see that even the mesh doesn't agree with itself about its own size;
You'll find that nrow(mesh$loc) and mesh$n are different although they
should be the same!!!

This is a strange bug as I don't see how it wasn't detected sooner; it
has to do with handling of "unused vertices" after the mesh
construction; these are removed, but it fails to update the "n"
element.

You can work around this in your code with
  mesh$n <- nrow(mesh$loc)

Let me know if that solves your problem; I've updated fmesher so that
from 0.1.2.9002 it should no longer have this bug.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I just checked the old INLA code, and that code handled this
differently and shouldn't be affected by the same problem, so you can
temporarily revert to that by using
  inla.setOption(fmesher.evolution=1L)
if needed.

Finn

On Wed, 27 Sept 2023 at 17:32, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I now see that even the mesh doesn't agree with itself about its own size;
> You'll find that nrow(mesh$loc) and mesh$n are different although they
> should be the same!!!
>
> This is a strange bug as I don't see how it wasn't detected sooner; it
> has to do with handling of "unused vertices" after the mesh
> construction; these are removed, but it fails to update the "n"
> element.
>
> You can work around this in your code with
>   mesh$n <- nrow(mesh$loc)
>
> Let me know if that solves your problem; I've updated fmesher so that
> from 0.1.2.9002 it should no longer have this bug.
>
> Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hallo Finn,

Yes! Thank you!
mesh$n <- nrow(mesh$loc) solved the problem!

"original"
summary(mesh)

Manifold: R2
CRS/LegacyPROJ4: +proj=utm +zone=33 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs

Interior segm.: 0

zlim: 0 0

with solution:
mesh$n <- nrow(mesh$loc)

Tested as well:
inla.setOption(fmesher.evolution=1L)
and this worked too.

I also tried it with the current version 0.1.2.9002. It works.

Thank you Finn for your work!

Best regards from Dresden.

Louis

You can do the same for a categorical covariate, except that you have a fixed effect for each level vs. the reference level, so you have to do it for each effect separately. Alternatively, it is possible to share a linear combination of fixed and/or random effects but that is done differently, I can provide more details if that sounds interesting to you.
Best,

messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,
I am wondering if the current version of R-INLA supports stationary spatial models inducing a Matérn covariance with a Mahalanobis distance instead of the Euclidean distance.
Also, is it possible to do a nonstationary analyis like this <https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0743> without getting one's hands too dirty ?
Kind regards and as always congrats for all your wonderful work
Sébastien

messages.subject: How does the number of high-level parameters impact the cost of INLA ?
messages.subject_clean: How does the number of high-level parameters impact the cost of INLA ?
messages.body_plain:
This question is completely unrelated with the one I just posted, but it is an interrogation I've had for a while and I think that the best answer is "from the horse's mouth".

>From the original paper of Rue, Martino, and Chopin, I understood that the collapsed maximum is found using quasi-Newton and then an exploration is done around the mode in order to determine credible intervals for the high level parameters and, correct me if I am wrong, compute credible intervals of the Gaussian effects of the model through various alternative procedures detailed in the paper. But if the space dimension goes higher, then the dimension of the high-density region around the node grows a lot. Also, I imagine that the quasi-Newton will suffer too. So, when does it start to hurt ?

Thank you all again
Sébastien

The first technique is just an adaptation of Haavard's example that you provided in the link of your first message for a continuous covariate. The second consists in adding a third likelihood that will correspond to the shared part between the two initial likelihoods. I made an example based on Haavard's code (see attached). In the context of a categorical covariate with 3 levels, you have the fixed effect of level 2 vs. level 1 (reference) and level 3 vs. level 1., i.e.:
eta1 =... + beta1*x1 + beta2*x2 + ...
eta2 = ...+ alpha1*(beta1*x1) + alpha2*(beta2*x2) + ...

Second option is doing:
eta1 =... + beta1*x1 + beta2*x2 + ...
eta2 = ...+ alpha*(beta1*x1+beta2*x2) + ...

Best,
Denis Rustand
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Is it possible to get an anisotropic Matérn model with INLA ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Is it possible to get an anisotropic Matérn model with INLA ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

there's no simple support for this at the moment (but some people may
have ad hoc code for it).

One of my PhD students is working on it (and others may be as well) as
we've figured out how to parameterise the anisotropy in a better way.

For _known_ anisotropy, you can mimic it by transforming your
coordinates and mesh; by stretching the mesh in a certain direction
before using it, you'll reduce the correlation range in that direction
in the original space, etc.

You can also obtain the fem matrices for essentially the model from
Fuglstad et al via fm_fem(mesh, aniso=list(gamma=...,vec=...)), and
use those in a direct call to inla.spde.generic(), but that's very
manual, and also requires known anisotropy.

Finn

The expected counts in area i are calculated as

Expected_i = Population_i * SumCasesAllAreas/SumPopulationAllAreas

replace the last line of code

Covid_Alab$Ei <- sum_population * Covid_Alab$ratio

by

Covid_Alab$Ei <- Covid_Alab$population* Covid_Alab$ratio

Best,
Paula
